title: Book 13 — Odysseus leaves Scheria and returns to Ithaca
paragraphs: He finished speaking, and everyone fell silent throughout the covered gallery, spellbound by the charm of his story, until Alcinous finally spoke up.

“Odysseus,” he said, “now that you’ve reached my house, I’m confident you’ll get home without any more trouble, no matter how much you’ve suffered before. But to the rest of you who come here night after night to drink my finest wine and listen to my bard, I want to say this: Our guest has already packed up the clothes, worked gold, and other treasures you’ve brought as gifts for him. Let’s now give him even more—each of us should contribute a large tripod and cauldron. We’ll reimburse ourselves through a general tax, since private individuals can’t be expected to bear the cost of such generous presents alone.”

Everyone agreed with this proposal, and then they all went home to bed. When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared, they hurried down to the ship carrying their cauldrons. Alcinous came aboard and made sure everything was securely stowed beneath the ship’s benches so nothing could break loose and injure the rowers. Then they went to Alcinous’s house for dinner, where he sacrificed a bull for them in honor of Zeus, lord of all. They grilled the meat and enjoyed an excellent feast, after which the inspired bard Demodocus, who was everyone’s favorite, sang for them. But Odysseus kept turning his eyes toward the sun, as if trying to make it set faster, for he was eager to be on his way. Like a man who has spent all day plowing a fallow field with a pair of oxen and thinks constantly of his supper, glad when night comes so he can go eat it—for his legs can barely carry him—just so did Odysseus rejoice when the sun went down. He immediately addressed the Phaeacians, speaking particularly to King Alcinous:

“Sir, and all of you, farewell. Make your drink offerings and send me on my way with joy, for you’ve fulfilled my heart’s desire by giving me an escort and these generous gifts. May heaven grant that I put them to good use. May I find my noble wife living peacefully among friends, and may you who remain here bring happiness to your own wives and children. May heaven grant you every blessing, and may no evil come to your people.”

Everyone approved his words and agreed he should have his escort since he had spoken so reasonably. Alcinous then said to his servant, “Pontonous, mix the wine and serve it to everyone, so we can pray to father Zeus and send our guest safely on his way.”

Pontonous mixed the wine and served it to each person in turn. The others poured their drink offerings from where they sat to the blessed gods that live in heaven, but Odysseus rose and placed the double cup in Queen Arete’s hands.

“Farewell, queen,” he said, “from now and forever, until old age and death—mankind’s common fate—lay their hands on you. I take my leave now. Be happy in this house with your children, your people, and King Alcinous.”

With these words he crossed the threshold, and Alcinous sent a man to escort him to his ship at the seashore. Arete also sent some maidservants with him—one carrying a clean shirt and cloak, another his strongbox, and a third with grain and wine. When they reached the water’s edge, the crew took these items and loaded them aboard along with all the food and drink. For Odysseus they spread a rug and linen sheet on the stern deck so he could sleep comfortably. Then he too came aboard and lay down without a word, while the crew took their positions and cast off the hawser from the pierced stone it had been tied to. As soon as they began rowing out to sea, Odysseus fell into a deep, sweet, almost deathlike sleep.

The ship bounded forward like a four-horse chariot racing over the course when the horses feel the whip. Her prow rose and fell like a stallion’s neck, and a great wave of dark blue water churned in her wake. She held steadily to her course, and even a falcon—swiftest of all birds—couldn’t have kept pace with her. So she cut through the water, carrying a man as cunning as the gods themselves, who now slept peacefully, forgetting all he had suffered both on the field of battle and on the waves of the weary sea.

When the bright star that heralds dawn’s approach began to show, the ship drew near to land. Now there is a harbor in Ithaca belonging to the old merman Phorcys, lying between two headlands that jut into the sea and shelter the harbor. These protect it from the storms and rough seas that rage outside, so that once inside, a ship can lie safely without even needing to be moored. At the head of this harbor stands a large olive tree, and nearby is a beautiful arching cave sacred to the nymphs called Naiads. Inside are stone mixing-bowls and wine jars, and bees make their hives there. There are also great stone looms where the nymphs weave their sea-purple robes—a wondrous sight to see—and there is always water within. The cave has two entrances: one facing north, by which mortals can enter, while the other faces south and is more mysterious—mortals cannot possibly enter by it, as it’s the path used by the gods.

Into this harbor they steered their ship, for they knew the place well. She had so much momentum that she ran half her own length onto the shore. Once they had landed, the first thing they did was lift Odysseus, still wrapped in his rug and linen sheet, out of the ship and lay him on the sand, still fast asleep. Then they unloaded the presents that Athena had persuaded the Phaeacians to give him for his homeward journey. They placed all these together by the olive tree’s roots, away from the road, in case some passerby might steal them before Odysseus woke up. Then they set off for home.

But Poseidon hadn’t forgotten the threats he had made against Odysseus, so he consulted with Zeus. “Father Zeus,” he said, “I’ll no longer be respected among the gods if mortals like the Phaeacians—who are my own descendants—show me so little regard. I said I would let Odysseus reach home after he had suffered enough. I didn’t say he should never get home at all, for I knew you had already nodded your agreement and promised he would. But now they’ve brought him home in a ship while he slept and landed him in Ithaca after loading him with more magnificent presents of bronze, gold, and fine clothing than he would ever have brought back from Troy, even if he’d gotten his fair share of the spoils and returned home without mishap.”

Zeus answered, “What are you talking about, Lord of the Earthquake? The gods certainly don’t lack respect for you. It would be outrageous for them to insult one so ancient and honored as you. As for mortals, if any of them treats you disrespectfully or acts insolently, you’re always free to deal with them as you see fit. Do whatever you please.”

“I would have acted at once,” replied Poseidon, “if I weren’t concerned about displeasing you. Now, however, I’d like to wreck the Phaeacian ship as it returns from its escort mission. This will stop them from escorting people in the future. I’d also like to bury their city under a huge mountain.”

“My good friend,” Zeus answered, “here’s what I’d recommend: at the very moment when people from the city are watching the ship return, turn it into a rock near the shore that looks like a ship. This will amaze everyone, and then you can bury their city under the mountain.”

When earth-encircling Poseidon heard this, he went to Scheria where the Phaeacians live and waited until the ship, which was making good speed, had gotten close to shore. Then he approached it, turned it to stone, and drove it down with his palm, rooting it firmly in the seabed. After this, he departed.

The Phaeacians began talking among themselves, and one would turn to his neighbor, saying, “Good heavens, who could have rooted our ship in the sea just as she was entering port? We could see all of her just a moment ago.”

This was how they spoke, but they knew nothing about what had really happened. Then Alcinous said, “I remember now the old prophecy my father told me. He said Poseidon would be angry with us for safely escorting everyone across the sea, and would one day wreck a Phaeacian ship returning from an escort mission and bury our city under a high mountain. That’s what my old father used to say, and now it’s all coming true. So let’s all do as I suggest: first, we must stop giving escorts to people who come here, and second, let’s sacrifice twelve choice bulls to Poseidon so he might have mercy on us and not bury our city under that high mountain.” When the people heard this, they were afraid and prepared the bulls.

So the chiefs and rulers of the Phaeacians prayed to King Poseidon, standing around his altar. At the same time, Odysseus woke up once more on his native soil. He had been away so long that he didn’t recognize it. Moreover, Zeus’s daughter Athena had made it a foggy day so people wouldn’t know of his arrival. She also wanted to tell him everything without his wife, fellow citizens, or friends recognizing him until he had taken revenge on the wicked suitors. Everything looked completely different to him—the long straight paths, the harbors, the cliffs, and the noble trees all appeared changed as he got up and looked upon his homeland. He struck his thighs with his palms and cried out in despair.

“Alas,” he exclaimed, “what kind of people have I fallen among? Are they savage and uncivilized, or hospitable and kind? Where shall I put all this treasure, and which way should I go? I wish I had stayed with the Phaeacians, or I could have gone to some other great chief who would have treated me well and given me an escort. As it is, I don’t know where to put my treasure, and I can’t leave it here for fear someone else might take it. Truly, the chiefs and rulers of the Phaeacians haven’t dealt fairly with me—they’ve left me in the wrong country! They said they would take me back to Ithaca, but they haven’t done so. May Zeus, protector of suppliants, chastise them, for he watches over everyone and punishes wrongdoers. Still, I suppose I should count my goods and see if the crew took any of them.”

He counted his fine copper vessels and cauldrons, his gold and all his clothes, but nothing was missing. Still, he kept grieving about not being in his own country and wandered up and down along the shore of the sounding sea, lamenting his harsh fate. Then Athena approached him, disguised as a young shepherd with a delicate, princely appearance. She wore a fine cloak folded double about her shoulders, had sandals on her lovely feet, and carried a javelin in her hand. Odysseus was glad when he saw her and went straight to her.

“My friend,” he said, “you’re the first person I’ve met in this country. I greet you and ask you to be kind to me. Protect both these goods of mine and me as well, for I clasp your knees and pray to you as if you were a god. Tell me truly—what land and country is this? Who lives here? Am I on an island, or is this the coastline of some continent?”

Athena answered, “Stranger, you must be very naive, or you must come from somewhere far away, not to know what country this is. It’s a very famous place, and everyone knows it, both east and west. It’s rugged and not good for driving horses, but it’s not a bad island for what it is. It grows plenty of grain and wine, for it gets both rain and dew. It breeds cattle and goats too. All kinds of trees grow here, and there are springs where the water never runs dry. So, sir, the name of Ithaca is known even as far as Troy, which I understand is a long way from this Achaean country.”
Odysseus was delighted to find himself, as Athena told him, in his own country, and he began to reply. But he didn’t tell the truth, instead making up a lying story with his instinctive cunning.

“I heard of Ithaca,” he said, “when I was in Crete across the sea, and now it seems I’ve reached it with all these treasures. I left just as much behind for my children, but I’m fleeing because I killed Orsilochus, son of Idomeneus, the fastest runner in Crete. I killed him because he tried to rob me of the spoils I’d won from Troy through so much trouble and danger, both on the field of battle and on the waves of the weary sea. He said I hadn’t served his father loyally at Troy as a vassal, but had set myself up as an independent ruler. So I ambushed him with one of my followers by the roadside and speared him as he was coming into town from the countryside. It was a very dark night and nobody saw us, so no one knew I had killed him. As soon as I’d done it, I went to a ship and begged the owners, who were Phoenicians, to take me aboard and set me down in Pylos or Elis where the Epeans rule, offering them spoils that satisfied them. They meant no harm, but the wind drove them off course, and we sailed until we arrived here by night. We could barely get into the harbor, and none of us mentioned supper though we badly wanted it. We all just went ashore and lay down as we were. I was exhausted and fell asleep immediately, so they took my goods from the ship and placed them beside me where I was lying on the sand. Then they sailed away to Sidonia, leaving me here in great distress.”

Such was his story, but Athena smiled and stroked him with her hand. Then she took the form of a woman—beautiful, tall, and wise. “He would have to be quite a shifty, lying fellow,” she said, “who could surpass you in all kinds of trickery, even if he were a god competing against you. You daredevil, full of schemes, never tiring of deception—can’t you drop your tricks and instinctive lies, even now that you’re back in your own country? But let’s say no more about this, since we can both deceive when the occasion calls for it. You’re the most accomplished counselor and speaker among all mortals, while I have no equal among the gods for diplomacy and cunning. Didn’t you recognize Zeus’s daughter Athena—me, who have always been with you, who watched over you through all your troubles, and who made the Phaeacians like you so much? And now I’ve come here again to discuss plans with you and help you hide the treasure I made the Phaeacians give you. I want to tell you about the troubles awaiting you in your own house. You’ll have to face them, but don’t tell anyone—man or woman—that you’ve returned home. Bear everything and endure every man’s insolence without a word.”

Odysseus answered, “A man may know a great deal, goddess, but you’re constantly changing your appearance, so when he meets you it’s hard to know whether it’s really you or not. This much I know for certain: you were very kind to me as long as we Achaeans were fighting before Troy. But from the day we boarded our ships after sacking Priam’s city and heaven scattered us—from that day, Athena, I saw no more of you and can’t remember you ever coming to my ship to help me in trouble. I had to wander on, sick and sorry, until the gods delivered me from evil and I reached the Phaeacians’ city, where you encouraged me and led me into town. Now I beg you in your father’s name, tell me the truth, for I don’t believe I’m really back in Ithaca. I must be in some other country, and you’re mocking and deceiving me with everything you’ve said. Tell me truly—have I really returned to my own land?”

“You’re always thinking something like that,” Athena replied, “and that’s why I can’t abandon you in your troubles—you’re so persuasive, shrewd, and shifty. Anyone else returning from such a long voyage would immediately rush home to see his wife and children, but you don’t seem to care about asking after them or hearing news about them until you’ve tested your wife, who stays at home grieving for you in vain, having no peace night or day for the tears she sheds on your account. As for my not coming near you, I was never worried about you, for I was certain you’d get home safely, though you’d lose all your men. I didn’t want to quarrel with my uncle Poseidon, who never forgave you for blinding his son. But now I’ll show you Ithaca’s landscape, and then perhaps you’ll believe me. This is the harbor of the old merman Phorcys, and here’s the olive tree that grows at its head. Near it is the cave sacred to the Naiads, and here’s the arching cavern where you’ve offered many acceptable sacrifices to the nymphs, and this is wooded Mount Neritum.”

As she spoke, the goddess dispersed the mist and the land appeared clearly. Then Odysseus rejoiced at finding himself in his own land again and kissed the fertile soil. He raised his hands and prayed to the nymphs, saying, “Naiad nymphs, daughters of Zeus, I was sure I would never see you again, so now I greet you with all loving salutations, and I’ll bring you offerings as in the old days, if Zeus’s formidable daughter grants me life and lets my son reach manhood.”
“Take heart and don’t worry about that,” Athena replied. “Let’s focus on storing your things safely in the cave right away. Let’s figure out how to manage this best.”

With that, she went down into the cave to look for the safest hiding places, while Odysseus brought up all the treasure of gold, bronze, and fine clothing the Phaeacians had given him. They stored everything carefully, and Athena placed a stone against the cave’s entrance. Then the two sat down by the great olive tree’s roots and planned how to destroy the wicked suitors.

“Odysseus,” Athena said, “noble son of Laertes, think about how you can lay hands on these shameless men who have been lording it in your house for three years, courting your wife and offering her wedding gifts, while she does nothing but mourn your absence, giving each of them hope and sending encouraging messages to all of them, but meaning the opposite of everything she says.”

Odysseus answered, “Truly, goddess, it seems I would have met the same terrible end in my own house as Agamemnon did, if you hadn’t given me this timely information. Advise me how I can best get my revenge. Stand by my side and fill my heart with courage, as you did on the day when we stripped Troy of her fair crown. Help me now as you did then, and I’ll fight three hundred men, if you, goddess, will be with me.”

“Trust me for that,” she said. “I won’t lose sight of you once we begin, and I imagine some of those who are devouring your wealth will then splatter the floor with their blood and brains. I’ll start by disguising you so no human will recognize you. I’ll cover your body with wrinkles, make you lose all your yellow hair, clothe you in a garment that will fill everyone who sees it with disgust, dim your fine eyes, and make you a repulsive sight to the suitors, your wife, and the son you left behind. Then go immediately to the swineherd who tends your pigs—he has always been loyal to you and devoted to Penelope and your son. You’ll find him feeding his pigs near the rock called Raven by the spring Arethusa, where they’re fattening on beech mast and spring water as is their way. Stay with him and find out how things stand, while I go to Sparta to see your son, who is with Menelaus in Lacedaemon, where he’s gone to try to learn whether you’re still alive.”
“But why,” Odysseus said, “didn’t you tell him, since you knew everything? Did you want him too to go sailing around facing all kinds of hardships while others devour his inheritance?”

Athena answered, “Don’t worry about him. I sent him so he’d gain a good reputation for having made the journey. He’s in no danger at all, but is staying quite comfortably with Menelaus, surrounded by every kind of abundance. The suitors have put out to sea and are waiting to ambush him, planning to kill him before he can get home. But I don’t think they’ll succeed—rather, some of those now devouring your estate will find their graves first.”

As she spoke, Athena touched him with her wand and covered him with wrinkles, took away all his yellow hair, and withered the flesh all over his body. She dimmed his eyes, which were naturally very fine, changed his clothes and threw a tattered old cloak around him, along with a tunic that was torn, filthy, and stained with smoke. She also gave him an untanned deerskin as an outer garment and provided him with a staff and a bag all in holes with a twisted thong to sling over his shoulder.
When the two had made their plans, they parted, and the goddess went straight to Lacedaemon to fetch Telemachus.
